content: Oxytocin is the most commonly used agent for labor induction worldwide. It can be administered alone, combined with amniotomy, or following cervical ripening achieved through other pharmacological or non-pharmacological methods. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of using oxytocin alone for cervical ripening and labor induction during the third trimester, comparing it to other induction methods or placebo/no treatment. The researchers conducted a systematic search of the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register (as of January 2009) and reviewed bibliographies of relevant studies. They included randomized and quasi-randomized trials that compared intravenous oxytocin with placebo, no treatment, or prostaglandins (administered vaginally or intracervically) for cervical ripening or labor induction in the third trimester. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility of studies and extracted data. A total of 61 trials involving 12,819 women were included in the analysis. When oxytocin induction was compared to expectant management (waiting for labor to begin naturally), fewer women failed to achieve vaginal delivery within 24 hours (8.4% with oxytocin versus 53.8% with expectant management; risk ratio [RR] 0.16, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.10 to 0.25). However, the use of oxytocin was associated with a significant increase in the need for epidural analgesia (RR 1.10, 95% CI 1.04 to 1.17). In one trial that assessed patient satisfaction, fewer women were dissatisfied with oxytocin induction compared to expectant management (5.9% versus 13.7%; RR 0.43, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.56). When oxytocin was compared to vaginal prostaglandins, the likelihood of unsuccessful vaginal delivery within 24 hours was higher with oxytocin (70% versus 21%; RR 3.33, 95% CI 1.61 to 6.89). Additionally, there was a slight increase in the use of epidurals when oxytocin was used alone (RR 1.09, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.17). Most of the studies included women with ruptured membranes. There was some evidence suggesting that vaginal prostaglandins increased the risk of maternal infection (chorioamnionitis; RR 0.66, 95% CI 0.47 to 0.92) and neonatal infection (as indicated by antibiotic use; RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.87). However, these findings should be interpreted cautiously, as infection was not a pre-specified outcome in the original review protocol. When oxytocin was compared to intracervical prostaglandins, the oxytocin group had a higher rate of unsuccessful vaginal delivery within 24 hours (50.4% versus 34.6%; RR 1.47, 95% CI 1.10 to 1.96) and a higher rate of cesarean sections (19.1% versus 13.7%; RR 1.37, 95% CI 1.08 to 1.74). In conclusion, the comparison of oxytocin with either intravaginal or intracervical prostaglandins suggests that prostaglandin agents may increase the likelihood of achieving vaginal delivery within 24 hours. However, oxytocin induction may lead to higher rates of labor interventions. There is also a suggestion that induction with vaginal prostaglandins in women with prelabor rupture of membranes may increase the risk of infection for both the mother and the baby, which warrants further investigation.
